DETAILED ACTION
This Non-Final Office Action is in response to claims filed 4/12/2022.
Claims 1-20 are pending.
Notice of Pre-AIA  or AIA  Status
The present application, filed on or after March 16, 2013, is being examined under the first inventor to file provisions of the AIA .
Information Disclosure Statement
The information disclosure statement (IDS) submitted on 12/20/2022 has been considered by the examiner.
Key to Interpreting this Office Action
For readability, all claim language has been underlined.
Citations from prior art are provided at the end of each limitation in parentheses.
Any further explanations that were deemed necessary by the Examiner are provided at the end of each claim limitation.
The Applicant is encouraged to contact the Examiner directly if there are any questions or concerns regarding the current Office Action.
Claim Objections
Claim 7 is objected to because of the following informalities:
Claim 7 recites wherein the transmitting a request for instructions to a tele-operation system, the request for the instructions which includes each candidate action of the set of candidate actions and each respective set of ancillary data includes transmitting a request for instructions to a tele-operation system, the request for the instructions which includes each respective probability and the order of preference (emphasis added). While it may be gleaned that the emphasized portion is further limiting a limitation of independent claim 1 provided as the un-emphasized portion, the claim language does not read well, due to a separate and distinct “request” being transmitted in the emphasized portion, and it cannot be reasonably determined if the “the request for instructions” of the emphasized portion is limiting the separate “request for instructions” in the emphasized portion or the “request for instructions” in the non-emphasized portion. In light of the Applicant’s disclosure, it is recommended to amend this limitation to read more clearly as “wherein the transmitted request for instructions includes each respective probability and the order of preference,” for example, or to provide proper antecedent basis.
Appropriate correction is required.
Claim Rejections - 35 USC § 103
In the event the determination of the status of the application as subject to AIA  35 U.S.C. 102 and 103 (or as subject to pre-AIA  35 U.S.C. 102 and 103) is incorrect, any correction of the statutory basis (i.e., changing from AIA  to pre-AIA ) for the rejection will not be considered a new ground of rejection if the prior art relied upon, and the rationale supporting the rejection, would be the same under either status.
The following is a quotation of 35 U.S.C. 103 which forms the basis for all obviousness rejections set forth in this Office action:
A patent for a claimed invention may not be obtained, notwithstanding that the claimed invention is not identically disclosed as set forth in section 102, if the differences between the claimed invention and the prior art are such that the claimed invention as a whole would have been obvious before the effective filing date of the claimed invention to a person having ordinary skill in the art to which the claimed invention pertains. Patentability shall not be negated by the manner in which the invention was made.
The factual inquiries for establishing a background for determining obviousness under 35 U.S.C. 103 are summarized as follows:
1. Determining the scope and contents of the prior art.
2. Ascertaining the differences between the prior art and the claims at issue.
3. Resolving the level of ordinary skill in the pertinent art.
4. Considering objective evidence present in the application indicating obviousness or nonobviousness.
Claims 1-20 are rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103 as being unpatentable over von Reventlow et al. (US 2023/0168670 A1), hereinafter von Reventlow, in view of alternative embodiments described in von Reventlow.
Claim 1
von Reventlow discloses the claimed method of operation of a robot (i.e. robot 1, depicted in Figure 1), the method performed by the robot (see ¶0044, regarding the embodiment in which processing unit 14 may be provided in robot 1), the method comprising:
identifying a set of candidate actions (i.e. action definition candidates) that may be performed by the robot (see ¶0008, regarding the processing unit automatically retrieves action definition candidates from a database according to a task);
collecting, for each candidate action of the set of candidate actions, a respective set of ancillary data (see ¶0008, regarding that the robot includes sensors for sensing the environment and determining the current situation for retrieving action definition candidates from the database; ¶0009-0010, regarding the calculation of a success score for each action definition candidate); “Ancillary data” is interpreted in light of the Applicant’s specification, defined as including sensor data or scores associated with a candidate action (see second paragraph on page 26 of the specification filed 4/12/2022).
transmitting a request for instructions to a tele-operation system, the tele-operation system communicatively coupled to the robot (see ¶0010-0011, regarding that the processing unit sends a request for assistance to a remote operator via a communication interface; ¶0054, with respect to Figure 2, regarding processing unit 14 sends the request for assistance via the communication interface 21 to the remote operation center, defined as including display 18 and input device 19, which communicate via operation center interface 21, in ¶0047), the request for the instructions which includes each candidate action of the set of candidate actions (see ¶0022, regarding that the request includes a plurality of action definition candidates);
receiving the instructions from the tele-operation system (see ¶0011, regarding that the system receives input from a remote operator);
executing the instructions (see ¶0011, regarding the robot will execute an action based on the input provided by the operator in response to the request for assistance); and
updating a control model (i.e. “knowledge base”) of the robot, based at least in part on each candidate action of the set of candidate actions, each respective set of ancillary data, and the instructions, to increase a level of autonomy of the robot (see ¶0011-0012, ¶0026, regarding that the corresponding action definition of the action executed based on remote controlled operation is stored in the database in association with the situation and its success score; ¶0083-0085, regarding that updating the database 17 improves the robot’s capability of autonomously executing a task).
Depending on the application of von Reventlow to the limitation of “ancillary data,” von Reventlow may further teach that the request for the instructions which includes…each respective set of ancillary data, in light of alternative embodiments within von Reventlow.
Specifically, in applying the sensed current situation described in ¶0008 of von Reventlow to the limitation of “ancillary data,” von Reventlow further teaches that a request for instructions includes each respective set of ancillary data (see ¶0066, regarding that all information collected by processing unit 14 from all available sensors is forwarded to the operator and output via display 18 as part of the request; ¶0016, regarding the sensor output is transmitted to the operator for deciding on the next operation of the robot). While von Reventlow particularly teaches the “request” as being associated with the unsegmented task in ¶0066, it would be reasonable to also conclude that the request for the instructions includes each respective set of ancillary data, in light of ¶0016, given that the sensor output is necessary for the operator to decide on the plurality of suggested action definition candidates (see ¶0022).
Therefore, it would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art before the effective filing date of the claimed invention to have modified the request for the instructions of von Reventlow, so as to further include each respective set of ancillary data, in light of ¶0016 and ¶0066 of von Reventlow, with the predictable result of enabling the operator to analyze the situation of the robot in order to decide on one of a plurality of suggested action definition candidates.
In applying the success scores described in ¶0009-0010 of von Reventlow to the limitation of “ancillary data,” von Reventlow further teaches that the request for the instructions includes action definition candidates defined by each respective set of ancillary data (see ¶0022, regarding that the request includes the plurality of action definition candidates with particular success scores for operator selection). Given that the “ancillary data” is a tool used for ranking/selection (see ¶0068-0069), it would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art before the effective filing date of the claimed invention to have modified the request for the instructions of von Reventlow to further include each respective set of ancillary data, in light of ¶0069 of von Reventlow, with the predictable result of providing the operator with additional information useful in deciding on the next operation.
Claim 2
von Reventlow further discloses that the robot comprising one or more sensors (see Figure 2, depicting microphone 22 and sensors 11, 12 on robot 1), wherein the identifying a set of candidate actions that may be performed by the robot includes sensing, by the one or more sensors, at least one of an external event or an external condition and identifying the set of candidate actions in response to sensing the at least one of an external event or an external condition (see ¶0006, regarding that the task is determined based on information sensed by the robot, where the action definition candidates are retrieved from the database based on the determined task, as described in ¶0008; ¶0057-0060).
Claim 3
von Reventlow further discloses receiving an objective (i.e. task) to be completed by the robot (see ¶0057, regarding that the task is determined through operator input, where a target state is defined by the task and may be changed by the operator, as described in ¶0073), wherein the identifying a set of candidate actions that may be performed by the robot includes identifying a set of candidate actions that may be performed by the robot in furtherance of the objective (see ¶0067, regarding the task is segmented into smaller pieces, each of which may correspond to a single action for which an action definition is stored in database 17).
While von Reventlow teaches the use of operator input, e.g., a smart phone or comparable device, for receiving an objective (see ¶0057), von Reventlow does not specifically teach that the objective is received from the tele-operation system. However, the “tele-operation system” of von Reventlow would be an obvious means of providing operator input, due to input device 19 provided in the remote operation center (see ¶0074, with respect to Figure 2, regarding input device 19 is used by the operator to provide input information and/or control signals for controlling the robot or instructing the use of action definitions).
It would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art before the effective filing date of the claimed invention to have modified the objective of von Reventlow to be received from the tele-operation system, in light of ¶0074 of von Reventlow, with the predictable result of defining a task through a known alternative operator input device for controlling a robot.
Claim 4
von Reventlow further discloses that the transmitting a request for instructions to a tele-operation system includes transmitting the request for instructions to the tele-operation system in response to determining the robot is unable to select a candidate action of the set of candidate actions to perform in furtherance of the objective (see ¶0022, regarding that requesting remote controlled operation in a case that the action definition candidates do not have a success score that indicates that the corresponding action may be executed successfully).
Claim 5
von Reventlow further discloses scoring each candidate action of the set of candidate actions (see ¶0009-0010, regarding that a success score is calculated for each retrieved action definition candidate, where the success score is a measure of how likely it is that an action according to an action definition candidate contributes to successfully fulfilling the task), wherein the scoring each candidate action of the set of candidate actions includes assigning a respective probability to each candidate action, the respective probability being based at least in part on a respective expectation of progress, achievable by each candidate action, towards the objective (see ¶0068, regarding that the success score may be a probability).
Claim 6
von Reventlow further discloses ranking each candidate action in an order of preference, the order of preference being based at least in part on the respective probability of each candidate action (see ¶0009-0010, regarding the determination of the action definition candidates with the highest scores for comparison to a threshold; ¶0068, regarding that the success score may be a probability). Due to the preference in selecting the action definition candidates with the highest scores, it is clear that the scores inherently represent a “ranking” of the respective action definition candidate.
Claim 7
von Reventlow is applied to the limitation of “ancillary data,” with respect to the success scores described in ¶0009-0010, as discussed in the second interpretation of “ancillary data” in the rejection of claim 1 above. Specifically, von Reventlow further discloses that the transmitting a request for instructions to a tele-operation system, the request for the instructions which includes each candidate action of the set of candidate actions data and each respective set of ancillary, as discussed in the rejection of claim 1, includes transmitting a request for instructions to a tele-operation system (see ¶0010-0011, regarding that the processing unit sends a request for assistance to a remote operator via a communication interface; ¶0054, with respect to Figure 2, regarding processing unit 14 sends the request for assistance via the communication interface 21 to the remote operation center, defined as including display 18 and input device 19, which communicate via operation center interface 21, in ¶0047).
von Reventlow further teaches the request for the instructions which includes action definition candidates defined by each respective probability and the order of preference (see ¶0022, regarding that the request includes the plurality of action definition candidates with particular success scores for operator selection; ¶0068, regarding that the success score may be a probability). Due to the preference in selecting the action definition candidates with the highest scores (see ¶0010-0011), it is clear that the scores inherently represent an “order of preference” of the respective action definition candidate. Given that the success score (probability) is a tool used for ranking/selection (see ¶0068-0069), it would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art before the effective filing date of the claimed invention to have modified the request for the instructions of von Reventlow to further include each respective probability and the order of preference, in light of ¶0069 of von Reventlow, with the predictable result of providing the operator with additional information useful in deciding on the next operation.
Claim 8
von Reventlow further discloses determining whether a respective probability meets a predetermined probability criterion (see ¶0068, regarding the success score, defined as a probability, is compared to a threshold to determine if the action is likely to be successfully applied in the current situation).
Claim 9
von Reventlow further discloses determining whether a difference between a first respective probability (i.e. success score for the determined action definition candidates) and a second respective probability (i.e. maximal achievable success score) meets a predetermined difference criterion (i.e. urgency indicator) (see ¶0075, regarding that the difference between the calculated success score for the determined action definition candidates and a maximal achievable success score is compared to an urgency indicator; ¶0068, regarding the success score is a probability).
Claim 10
von Reventlow further discloses the robot being a semi-autonomous robot characterized by a level of autonomy (see ¶0010-0011, regarding the autonomous control of the robot when the success score is above a threshold and the remote operator control of the robot when the success score is below a threshold), the level of autonomy being determined at least in part by the control model (see ¶0011-0012, ¶0026, regarding that the corresponding action definition of the action executed based on remote controlled operation is stored in the database in association with the situation and its success score; ¶0083-0085, regarding that updating the database 17 improves the robot’s capability of autonomously executing a task). “Level of autonomy” may be broadly interpreted, and the success scores of the action definition candidates reasonably reflect a level of autonomy, given that the success scores are the basis for determining manual or autonomous operation of an action (see ¶0010).
von Reventlow further discloses the method further comprising comparing the level of autonomy of the robot to a threshold level of autonomy, the threshold level of autonomy above which the robot is operable to autonomously select a candidate action of the set of candidate actions to perform (see ¶0010, ¶0069, regarding that the robot automatically executes the action associated with an action definition candidate with the highest success score of all evaluated action definition candidates). The “threshold level of autonomy” may be reasonably taught by the threshold used to compare with the success score of an action definition candidate, in which the decision of autonomous operation depends. von Reventlow further discloses that the transmitting a request for instructions to a tele-operation system includes transmitting the request for instructions to the tele-operation system in response to determining the level of autonomy of the robot is lower than the threshold level of autonomy (see ¶0010-0011, regarding that the processing unit sends a request for assistance to a remote operator via a communication interface when the success score is below the threshold).
Claim 11
von Reventlow further teaches in response to determining the level of autonomy of the robot meets or exceeds the threshold level of autonomy, performing one of the candidate actions of the set of candidate actions (see ¶0074, regarding autonomously executing actions with success scores above the threshold).
Claim 12
von Reventlow further discloses receiving an objective (i.e. task) to be completed by the robot (see ¶0057, regarding that the task is determined through operator input, where a target state is defined by the task and may be changed by the operator, as described in ¶0073), wherein the identifying a set of candidate actions that may be performed by the robot includes identifying a set of candidate actions that may be performed by the robot in furtherance of the objective (see ¶0067, regarding the task is segmented into smaller pieces, each of which may correspond to a single action for which an action definition is stored in database 17).
While von Reventlow teaches the use of operator input, e.g., a smart phone or comparable device, for receiving an objective (see ¶0057), von Reventlow does not specifically teach that the objective is received from the tele-operation system. However, the “tele-operation system” of von Reventlow would be an obvious means of providing operator input, due to input device 19 provided in the remote operation center (see ¶0074, with respect to Figure 2, regarding input device 19 is used by the operator to provide input information and/or control signals for controlling the robot or instructing the use of action definitions).
It would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art before the effective filing date of the claimed invention to have modified the objective of von Reventlow to be received from the tele-operation system, in light of ¶0074 of von Reventlow, with the predictable result of defining a task through a known alternative operator input device for controlling a robot.
Claim 13
von Reventlow further teaches determining the threshold level of autonomy, wherein the determining the threshold level of autonomy includes assigning a respective probability to each candidate action, the respective probability being based at least in part on a respective expectation of progress, achievable by each candidate action, towards the objective (see ¶0009-0010, regarding that a success score defined as a probability in ¶0068 is calculated for each retrieved action definition candidate, where the success score is a measure of how likely it is that an action according to an action definition candidate contributes to successfully fulfilling the task).
Claim 14
von Reventlow further discloses ranking each candidate action in an order of preference, the order of preference being based at least in part on the respective probability (see ¶0009-0010, regarding the determination of the action definition candidates with the highest scores for comparison to a threshold; ¶0068, regarding that the success score may be a probability). Due to the preference in selecting the action definition candidates with the highest scores, it is clear that the scores (probabilities) inherently represent a “ranking” of the respective action definition candidate.
Claim 15
von Reventlow further teaches that the determining the level of autonomy of the robot is lower than the threshold level of autonomy includes determining the respective probability of each candidate action in the set of candidate actions fails to satisfy at least one predetermined criterion (see ¶0068, regarding that the success score, defined as a probability, is compared to a threshold to determine if the action is likely to be successfully applied in the current situation).
Claim 16
von Reventlow further discloses the robot comprising one or more sensors (see ¶0043, with respect to sensor depicted in Figure 2) and a data repository (see ¶0008-0009, regarding the retrieval of action definition candidates from a database by the processing unit, so as to evaluate and calculate a success score). It is clear that a memory or buffer is used by the processing unit of the robot to perform evaluations and calculations of the action definition candidates. von Reventlow further discloses that the collecting, for each candidate action of the set of candidate actions, a respective set of ancillary data includes at least one of collecting a first subset of the respective set of ancillary data by the one or more sensors or extracting a second subset of the respective set of ancillary data from the data repository (see ¶0008, regarding that the robot includes sensors for sensing the environment and determining the current situation for retrieving action definition candidates from the database; ¶0008-0010, regarding the calculation of a success score for each action definition candidate from a database). As discussed in the rejection of claim 1, “ancillary data” is interpreted in light of the Applicant’s specification, defined as including sensor data or scores associated with a candidate action (see second paragraph on page 26 of the specification filed 4/12/2022).
Claim 17
von Reventlow further discloses that the transmitting a request for instructions to a tele-operation system includes transmitting a request for the tele-operation system to determine which candidate action the robot should perform (see ¶0022, regarding the operator selects one of the suggested action definition candidates in response to the request).
Claim 18
von Reventlow further discloses the robot comprising a motion actuator (see ¶0007, regarding that the robot moves using its drive system; ¶0045, with respect to Figure 2, regarding actuators 16 are controlled by driver 15 of robot 1), wherein executing the instructions includes causing, by the motion actuator, the robot to execute a movement (see ¶0018, regarding that the action definition is any kind of motion that is executed by the robot).
Claim 19
von Reventlow further discloses the updating a control model, based at least in part on each candidate action of the set of candidate actions, each respective set of ancillary data, and the instructions includes increasing a level of autonomy of the robot from a first level of autonomy to a second level of autonomy, the second level of autonomy being higher than the first level of autonomy (see ¶0083-0085, regarding that updating the database 17 improves the robot’s capability of autonomously executing a task). “Levels of autonomy” may be broadly interpreted, and increasing autonomous capability in von Reventlow may reasonably be interpreted as increasing from a “first level” to a “second level,” due to the levels being undefined in the claim.
Claim 20
von Reventlow further discloses identifying, by the robot, an objective (i.e. task) to be completed by the robot (see ¶0006, regarding that the robot determines a task; ¶0057-0059), wherein the identifying a set of candidate actions that may be performed by the robot includes identifying a set of candidate actions that may be performed by the robot in furtherance of the objective (see ¶0067, regarding the task is segmented into smaller pieces, each of which may correspond to a single action for which an action definition is stored in database 17).
Conclusion
